Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette:
Huy Tran, a 76-year-old single warehouse worker from Southeast Asia, came to treatment after years of managing his symptoms by keeping busy and keeping quiet. He described being a young civilian in a war zone, caught in the middle of a street raid when soldiers pinned him face-down against the ground and held his arms behind him. The smell of sweat, dust, and fuel mixed with the wet earth under his cheek, and the scene had imprinted itself so clearly that, decades later, he could still picture the rough boots, the shape of the wall beside him, and the sound of shouting as though it were happening again. Huy said that now, without warning, something in his surroundings can bring the whole memory back with startling force: a whiff of diesel near the loading bay, the sharp odor of damp cardboard, or the moment a coworker grips his shoulders too firmly in a crowded aisle. When that happens, he is no longer just remembering; he is flooded by the same fear and helplessness, and he has to stop whatever he is doing because the feeling becomes too overwhelming to push through.

For Huy, these moments of recall are especially tied to being restrained or cornered. If a supervisor comes up behind him unexpectedly or if another worker blocks his path during a disagreement, the old scene arrives instantly and with full detail, as vivid and precise as a photograph he never wanted to keep. The memory is not vague or distant; he notices every sensory piece at once, from the smell that seems to cling to his clothes to the pressure of being held down, and that clarity makes the experience feel immediate rather than past. He has come to believe that his mind is never far from it, waiting for the right cue, and that is part of what has made ordinary moments at the warehouse feel dangerous.

In turn, once the memory surfaces, Huy becomes far more alert to anything that might set it off again. He watches the people around him closely, especially in the narrow storage lanes where someone might brush past him or reach for a box behind him, and he tries to avoid confrontations at work because raised voices and tense exchanges can pull him back into the same state. He keeps a careful distance during disagreements, lets minor slights pass, and often volunteers for solitary tasks near the loading dock so he will not have to stand shoulder to shoulder with others or be touched unexpectedly. He said the smell of certain oils and fuel mixtures on the warehouse floor can make him tense before he even knows why, and once the memory starts, he scans for every possible sign that it could happen again. That vigilance has narrowed his days; he works, but with less ease and less willingness to speak up, and he has grown quieter with the few people he sees regularly.

Over time, the cycle has made his world smaller. Huy misses breaks when the lunchroom is crowded and avoids areas where tempers rise, even if that means taking longer routes through the building or staying late to finish tasks after others leave. He has noticed that the more he tries to prevent another surge of memory, the more exhausting the day becomes, because he is always bracing for a smell, a grip on his arm, or a confrontation that might bring everything back. The clarity of the memory gives the triggers their force, and the force of the triggers keeps the memory close. By the time he sought help, it was after he found himself frozen one afternoon when a younger worker jokingly grabbed him by the elbows near a pallet jack and the odor of solvent from a nearby aisle hit him at the same moment. Huy finally came because he is tired of living as though his body is still on that street, and what he most fears is being caught off guard again and overwhelmed so completely that he cannot keep working, or cannot keep himself steady in front of other people. He hopes, more than anything, to move through his warehouse days without the old scene seizing him whole.
